Sub-events.Sub-event: German Recognition of Vulnerability and Initial Response to American Bridgehead, 7 July 1944
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: German commanders identify a weak point in defenses between Taute and Vire Rivers after American bridgehead establishment. Seventh Army shifts minor forces westward; Panzer Lehr selected for delayed counterattack; part of 2d SS Panzer Division redirected eastward to hold until Panzer Lehr arrives.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_1: The comparative ease with which the bridgehead between the Taute and the Vire Rivers was established on 7 July indicated to Americans and Germans alike the existence of a soft spot in the German defenses. With only Kampfgruppe Heinz and a small part of the 17th SS Panzer Grenadier Division defending the area, the Americans were close to achieving a breakthrough. Hausser, the Seventh Army commander, shifted a mobile (bicycle) brigade of light infantry and a reconnaissance battalion westward across the Vire River out of the II Parachute Corps sector. This could be only an expedient, a stopgap measure, for obviously the troops were not strong enough, nor the defensive attitude that their commitment implied sufficient, to stop expansion of the bridgehead. What the Germans needed was a counterattack by strong forces to demolish the bridgehead and restore the positions along the canal and the river.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_2: Panzer Lehr, an armored division recently in defensive positions near Caen, seemed to Kluge and Rommel an obvious choice. Having just been replaced by a newly arrived infantry division, Panzer Lehr was scheduled to go into the Panzer Group West reserve and strengthen Eberbach's zone defense. The division was the only strong force available for transfer to the Seventh Army front to counterattack the American bridgehead.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_3: Since shifting the division across the front from the vicinity of Caen to the area west of St. Lô would take several days, the Germans had to preserve the conditions that still made a counterattack feasible. They had to find strong forces that were closer to the threatened area and available for immediate commitment. They settled on the 2d SS Panzer Division, most of which already was battling the VII and VIII Corps. Although Kluge realized that drawing part of the SS armored division away from the Seventh Army left might weaken the west flank defenses beyond repair, Rommel pointed out that the Taute and Vire situation was much more critical. American success between the two rivers had created a minor penetration that, if exploited, might well invalidate the German policy of holding fast. Kluge reluctantly agreed. He approved the plan to send part of the 2d SS Panzer Division eastward across the Taute to hold until the Panzer Lehr Division, moving westward across the Vire, could arrive to counterattack and demolish the bridgehead.

Sub-events.Sub-event: American Reinforcement and Conflicting Intentions for Exploitation, 7 July 1944
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Americans reinforce bridgehead with 3d Armored Division from army reserve. General Bradley directs support for 30th Division. General Corlett instructs armored commander to cross Vire and drive south aggressively, but conflicting visions emerge among army, corps, and division levels, leading to initial confusion.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_4: The Americans, for their part, having judged the probable German course correctly, hastened to exploit their success before the enemy could act. Hopeful that the First Army offensive was at last about to move with dispatch, but also looking to the lesser goal of shoring up the bridgehead against counterattack, General Bradley gave XIX Corps the 3d Armored Division, which had been in the army reserve. Unwilling to dictate the details of commitment, General Bradley simply instructed General Corlett to support the 30th Division with the armored division.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_5: General Corlett had definite ideas of his own. He wanted to get the 3d Armored Division across the Vire, pass it through the 30th Division, and advance rapidly to the south to seize and hold the high ground west of St. Lô. Unfortunately, it was difficult to translate the desire into action, for General Corlett was severely ill and confined to bed at his command post for several days. He telephoned the armored division commander, Maj. Gen. Leroy H. Watson, in the late afternoon of 7 July and instructed him to cross the Vire River as soon as he could and then drive south. "How far do you want me to go?" General Watson asked. "The Germans have little or nothing over there," the corps commander replied, "just keep going."
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_6: Thus, at the beginning of the new phase of action between the Taute and the Vire, clarity of aims was lacking. The army commander envisioned a build-up of the bridgehead forces with armor; the corps commander foresaw a limited exploitation to the ridge west of St. Lô; the armored division commander understood that he was to make an unlimited drive to the south. The incompatibility of intent led to some confusion that was the beginning of increasing disorder.

Sub-events.Sub-event: Commitment of 3d Armored Division CCB and Initial Movement Challenges, 7-8 July 1944
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: 3d Armored Division (old-type organization) commits CCB under Brig. Gen. John J. Bohn. Delayed crossing of Vire at Airel bridge due to congestion, enemy fire, and shared use with 30th Division; units face harassment upon entry into bridgehead.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_7: Although General Corlett had known for some time that the armored division might be attached to his corps, illness prevented him from personally directing its commitment. To help him with the operation, Maj. Gen. Walton H. Walker, commander of the XX Corps, which had not yet been committed to action, temporarily acted as Corlett's representative. General Watson was surprised by the sudden news of his impending commitment. ... Watson decided to send one combat command across the river first.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_8: General Watson's force was one of the two "old-type" armored divisions ... Watson's decision to commit one combat command as a start was normal.

Sub-events.Sub-event: Relief of Bohn, Renewal Under Roysdon, and Seizure of Hauts-Vents, 10-11 July 1944
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: General Bohn relieved for lack of aggressiveness. Colonel Roysdon assumes command. Advance resumes with difficulty; Hill 91 seized on 11 July after multiple attempts despite losses and German resistance from Panzer Lehr.
